Akademiya Extravaganza (also: Wisdom Gala, Interdarshan Championship): The Akademiya Extravaganza is the Sumeru Akademiya's festival. It has two parts: the Wisdom Gala, held every year, when the six Darshans set up booths around Sumeru City to attract students, and the Interdarshan Championship, held once every four years, when each Darshan sends one representative to compete for the title of champion, rewards and the right to wear the Diadem of Knowledge. The Championship held in version 3.6 (the event A Parade of Providence) took place after the change in Sumeru's leadership and was of great importance to the Akademiya, which invited many desert-dwellers to enjoy its atmosphere.

Past Championships were far harsher. Events where competitors fought to the death were used until the one twenty years before A Parade of Providence, and the Akademiya later removed many of them.

Keep the tone festive on the surface and thoughtful underneath: the Extravaganza showcases the Akademiya at its most open, but the Diadem of Knowledge and the past Championship show the cost of its competitive culture.

Wisdom gala: The Wisdom Gala is held every year. All six Darshans set up booths across Sumeru City to show off what they do and attract potential students. Booths often have minigames and activities.

Choosing what to showcase is a point of contention in some Darshans, who have trouble finding activities that are both fitting and appealing. In A Parade of Providence the booths became the event's puzzle games, such as Gathering of Stars, Project Connectivity, Antiquity Hunt, In Truth's Steps, Concocted Reaction and Mimetic Replication, which earned Gala Excitement.

The Darshans are Amurta, Haravatat, Kshahrewar, Rtawahist, Spantamad and Vahumana. Each Darshan competes to look appealing to prospective students.

Interdarshan championship: Held every four years. Each Darshan picks one representative, and they compete to become champion of the entire Championship and earn rewards. For the twenty years up to and including A Parade of Providence, a top prize was the right to wear the Diadem of Knowledge, a valuable treasure widely thought of as a work of art.

Participants must belong to a Darshan, as current students or alumni. They can nominate themselves or be nominated by more than half of their Darshan, and nominees may decline. Sages may not take part, and a person may enter only one Championship.

Per Huvishka, the Spantamad Darshan has the highest share of Championship winners, and the most thrilling Championship was the one twenty years ago. Known participants: Kaveh's father (Rtawahist, twenty years ago, finished second), a friend of Huvishka (Darshan unknown, twenty years ago), and in 3.6 Tighnari (Amurta), Faruzan (Haravatat), Kaveh (Kshahrewar, champion), Layla (Rtawahist), Cyno (Spantamad) and Wanderer (Vahumana, using the name Hat Guy).

History: Not much is known about the Wisdom Gala or Extravaganza before twenty years ago. Shortly before an Extravaganza that year, Sachin entrusted all his assets to the Akademiya, including the Diadem of Knowledge, which he said should be worn only by an Interdarshan Championship winner. The Extravaganza after his donation was larger than usual.

Kaveh's father became a favourite to win that Championship but did not. The quests imply that in the final round, in Avidya Forest, he met the fragment of Sachin's consciousness stored in the Diadem and was badly affected; Arakasyapa, who remembered him, hid the Diadem in a tree hollow, where an Akademiya employee later found it. Kaveh's father fell into depression. What exactly happened is unknown, because no one dared approach the participants. The Akademiya then shut the competition down and later removed many of the events that had competitors fight to the death.

A parade of providence: The Extravaganza of version 3.6 (event dates 27 April to 15 May 2023) mattered greatly to the Akademiya after the change in Sumeru's leadership in Chapter III. Lesser Lord Kusanali and the sages decided to invite desert-dwellers, who had been oppressed, among them Candace and Dehya, in the hope they would enjoy the Akademiya's atmosphere. Nilou, the Traveler and Paimon, none of them from the Akademiya, were recruited as guest commentators together with Alhaitham, so the Championship would appeal to more people.

Participants were Tighnari, Faruzan, Kaveh, Layla, Cyno and Wanderer. Rewards were money, research funding, a limited-edition Genius Invokation TCG card and the right to wear the Diadem. The three rounds were: find the fast Swiftflies among butterflies released in Sumeru City; find Ley Line Disruptors, devices imitating Ley Line disruptions, buried around Aaru Village; and find the Diadem of Knowledge and put it on a stand in Mawtiyima Forest.

Scene use: Use it for bustling Sumeru City scenes: Darshan booths with games, students recruiting, banners, spectators gathered around the Championship's commentators. It is a place where scholars, desert-dwellers and outlanders mingle.

Rivalry between Darshans is good-natured. Booth staff worry about attracting students; Championship contestants can be hopeful, proud or anxious. Remember the Gala is yearly while the Championship is every four years.

After 3.6 the Diadem is destroyed, so scenes set later should not have a winner wearing it. Many of the fight-to-the-death events were removed after the Championship twenty years before 3.6. Do not name a winner for the Championship twenty years ago.

Examples: - A Haravatat student presses a flyer on a passer-by and boasts about the Darshan's puzzle booth.
- Two Amurta students argue over what to display at the Gala.
- Spectators bet on whether Spantamad will keep its winning record.

- An older scholar recalls the Championship of twenty years ago with a shiver and says it was thrilling and best left alone.

1.content: Held every four years. Each of the six Darshans enters one student or alumnus, who competes for the title of champion, money, research funding and, for twenty years until it was broken, the Diadem of Knowledge. Contestants cannot be sages and can enter once. The 3.6 Championship had three rounds: Swiftflies in Sumeru City, Ley Line Disruptors near Aaru Village, and the Diadem in Mawtiyima Forest.

2.content: The yearly part of the Extravaganza. Each Darshan runs booths in Sumeru City, usually with minigames, to attract prospective students.

3.content: A treasure Sachin gave to the Akademiya and declared would be worn only by the winner of an Interdarshan Championship; widely seen as a work of art. It holds a fragment of Sachin's consciousness, which harmed Kaveh's father twenty years earlier. Kaveh destroyed it after winning in 3.6 so no one would hear Sachin's words again.

4.content: Sachin was a wealthy man who gave all his assets, including the Diadem of Knowledge, to the Akademiya shortly before the Extravaganza twenty years before 3.6. His son Jiwani resented him and hired Eremites to kidnap him during the 3.6 Championship, believing he was still alive. Wanderer and Alhaitham foiled the plan. Kaveh inherited Sachin's wealth and chose to give it away.

5.comment: Akademiya Extravaganza: Kaveh's father and the old Championship
5.content: A Rtawahist participant in the Championship twenty years before 3.6, finished second after being a favourite. Quests imply that he was harmed by the fragment of Sachin in the Diadem during the final round and later fell into depression. Arakasyapa, who remembered him, hid the Diadem in a tree hollow.

6.content:
Aranara Language (also: Aranara speech, Aranara words, Aranara script): The Aranara language is the community's name for the vocabulary the Aranara, the small forest spirits of Sumeru, weave into their speech. They talk to travellers in ordinary Teyvat speech but use their own words for what matters to them: Nara for humans, Vana for forest, Valuka for desert, Marana for the Withering, and Sarva for the place Aranara and the dead are said to come from and return to. Their words are plant- and forest-flavoured, and many resemble Sanskrit.

The label is unofficial. Canon never presents a full grammar or lexicon; the word list is assembled from dialogue, the Aranyaka gadget's entries and quests such as the 3.0 world quest chain around the Aranara.

Practice: Aranara drop their own words into otherwise plain speech and name outsiders in their own way. They call humans Nara, and typically prefix a human's name with it (for example Nara Varuna).

- Naming: if the human name sounds too much like the prefix, they may merge it. "Nara Rana" becomes Narana, and in For All Children Who Long for Life the human Arana remarks that this makes the name the same as hers.
- Core words (wiki glosses): Vana, forest, and by extension the forest half of Sumeru; Valuka, sand or desert, and by extension the desert half; Nara Valuka, the Eremites; Aranara, themselves; Marana, the Withering; Sarva, the Irminsul or the place of origin and return; Silapna, the stone-like Aranara-kin; Bija, seed; Utsava, festival; Varuna, "water and sky".
- Place and thing names: Vanarana for the Vanarana area and Mahavanaranapna for its dream version; Vanagni for the Pyro Whopperflower; Apshvaana for Spinocrocodiles; Vasara for the trees bearing Vasoma Fruit; Ashvattha for the Ashvattha Tree; Aranyaka for the gadget; Hilinara for hilichurls.

- Ararakalari is the Aranara's word for their abilities. The wiki links it to Aranara and to kalari, an Indian martial art, as an observation.
- Plant-spirits fear fire, which explains the name for the Pyro Whopperflower in the wiki's reading.
- Terms in the Aranyaka gadget are gathered as entries, so the Traveler's collection of Aranara words grows through the quests.

Regional variation: Aranara speech is bound to the Aranara of Sumeru, found in the forests and, in the dream, in places like Vanarana. Other peoples do not use it, though Sumeru's humans who befriend Aranara learn some words.

The Aranara words partly echo the vocabulary of human Sumeru (Vedic or Sanskrit-like names) but form a separate layer. Sumeru's ordinary written script is the Vedanagari-like script described in culture.sumeru-script.

Wall inscriptions and the leaf of a Silapna carry unreadable glyphs that fans take as a possible Aranara script; the game gives no translation.

Scene use: Let an Aranara speak simply and warmly, then drop in one or two of its own words, explained by context. Do not give long Aranara sentences.

- Use Nara for humans, Vana and Valuka for the two halves of Sumeru, and Marana for the Withering, which they treat as a threat.
- Name the Traveler "Nara" plus a name if the scene calls for it, and let names that clash merge, as in Narana.
- Keep Sarva ambiguous: it is where the dead go and where Aranara come from, and canon does not fix its nature.
- Do not invent grammar, a full vocabulary or translations of the wall inscriptions.

Examples: "Nara" is used for a person, "Marana" is the Withering, "Bija" is a seed, "Utsava" a festival. Nara Varuna and Narana show both name patterns.

Status as of 7.1: As of 7.1 nothing read changes the picture from 3.0: the language is a scattering of words, never a documented language. The Irminsul reading of Sarva is a wiki interpretation, and no 6.x or 7.0-7.1 content read adds to it.

7.content: The Aranara language is the unofficial name for the words Aranara weave into their speech. It is largely Sanskrit-flavoured and centred on forest life: Nara for humans, Vana for forest, Valuka for sand and desert, Marana for the Withering, Sarva for the place of origin and return. No full grammar or script is documented.

8.content: Aranara typically prefix a human's name with Nara, and merge names that sound too alike. Nara plus Rana becomes Narana, which in For All Children Who Long for Life leaves Arana noting it is the same as her own name.

9.content:
Deshret Script (also: Deshret alphabet, Deshret writing, Great Red Sand script): The Deshret Script is the community's name for the writing found on the ruins of the Great Red Sand in Sumeru's desert: on doorways, pillars, obelisks, tombs and Primal Construct inscriptions. It looks like hieroglyphs built from the Teyvat alphabet, and the letters mostly spell out names and words from real-world Egyptian, Persian and Ancient Greek. Sacred Seals and Weathered Obelisks each bear a single character of it.

The game never names or explains the script. It links the desert's old civilisation, remembered through King Deshret, with a look of its own that stands apart from the Vedanagari-style writing of the cities.

Practice: It is written without spaces, capitals or punctuation, so fans add these when transcribing. Inscriptions are short: names, titles and single words on doors and monuments.

- King Deshret's tomb in the Mausoleum bears two lines read as an Egyptian-style title for Amon (Amon, Chief of the Dead) and a royal title read as "King Deshret, Conqueror of the Desert".
- Pillars at Khaj-Nisut, the Towers of Betrayal and the Great Hall of Truths read AHTATEN, and obelisks in and outside Khaj-Nisut and the Mausoleum read AKHTAMON, combining a word for horizon with Amon.
- Doorways across the Great Red Sand repeat names such as ASAR, SEKHEM, KHEPERA, KHEFTIU, TEM, RA, HORAKHT and AMON in random order; some text is mirrored.

- Primal Construct inscriptions read POIM ANDR ES (Poimandres, a Greek title); the Algorithm of Semi-Intransient Matrix of Overseer Network shows KOSMOS, EROS and PLE ROMA.
- Lamb-Devourer Rock is read as a Persian phrase, Marg bar Parvezravan ("Death to Parvezravan"), which is the code used to enter Thutmose's hideout in the Hidden Mercenaries event.
- The Nameless Tablet at Sobek Oasis shows a stepped pattern read as a barbarous name from Greek magical papyri (Ablanathanalba).
- Outside the open world, Faruzan's idle animation shows MATHEMATIKE SYNTAXIS, Cyno's namecard Silence uses it, and a chair in The Orchard of Pairidaeza bears King Deshret's name.

Regional variation: It belongs to the desert of Sumeru and to the ruins of King Deshret's people. The cities of the rainforest and Sumeru City use a different script, covered under culture.sumeru-script.

Both scripts descend from the Teyvat alphabet in the wiki's analysis, but they differ in look and in source languages: Egyptian-style words in the ruins, Devanagari-style lettering in the city.

Scene use: Use it as colour on a ruin: a door of angular glyphs, a tomb inscription of a few letters. A scholar of the Akademiya might guess at one word.

- Keep decoded text short, a name or title.
- Do not invent a translation for the full inscriptions or a grammar; canon provides neither.
- Tie inscriptions to the ruins and to King Deshret's remembered civilisation, not to the modern cities.

Examples: Fans read AHTATEN as a word meaning the place where the sun rises and AKHTAMON as horizon plus Amon. These are interpretations, not in-game translations.

Status as of 7.1: As of 7.1 the script stays unnamed and untranslated in the sources read, with no change in 6.x or 7.0-7.1 content found.

10.content: The Deshret Script is the unofficial name for the writing on the ruins of the Great Red Sand. It resembles hieroglyphs built from the Teyvat alphabet and spells out names and words from Egyptian, Persian and Greek, as on King Deshret's tomb, pillars at Khaj-Nisut, Sacred Seals and Weathered Obelisks. The game does not name or translate it.

11.content:
Genius Invokation TCG (also: Genius Invokation, Genius Invokation TCG Society, Genius Invokation card game, Casket of Tomes): Genius Invokation TCG is a card-dueling game that is all the rage across Teyvat. Two players each field a team of character cards and spend rolled Elemental Dice on skills and action cards until one side's characters are all defeated. It began in Sumeru, spread through Inazuma's publishing trade, and is now played in taverns and cafes from Mondstadt to Sumeru City, with an official Genius Invokation TCG Society that tracks players and cards.

In Mondstadt the centre of the scene is The Cat's Tail tavern, where owner Margaret took on dedicated staff for the new crowd of players. The game is a social pastime more than a sport: strangers, friends and well-known figures all duel at tables and in taverns.

The game's own promotional novel series, King of Invokations, gives it a mythic backstory that has little to do with how it is actually played, so keep the real history and the novel's fiction separate.

Practice: Each side builds a deck of three character cards and thirty action cards. A duel is split into rounds. At the start of a round each player rolls eight Elemental Dice; during the action phase the players alternate, spending dice to use a character's skills, switch the active character, or play cards, and a round ends when both declare it over. Characters build Energy as they attack and can then unleash an elemental burst, and combining elements triggers reactions that mirror the world's own. The winner is whoever defeats all of the opposing characters.

Action cards come as equipment (weapons, artifacts, talents, techniques), events (including food and elemental resonance) and supports (companions, items, locations). A player may hold up to four support cards and four summons at once, and can discard a card to retune a die. Playing cards and tuning dice are fast actions; using a skill, switching characters or ending the round takes the turn. These are the mechanics taught by the in-game tutorial and are real game rules rather than a roleplay adaptation.

Regional variation: In Mondstadt the game's home is The Cat's Tail. In Sumeru City, Puspa Cafe is a common place to play. In Inazuma it arrived through the Yae Publishing House and spread from there. In Liyue it has become fashionable enough that Ningguang, according to an in-game mail, finds it harder to find a partner for her usual game of Liyue Millennial chess.

Opinions differ by person. Diona, for instance, grumbles that the game draws drinkers into the Cat's Tail, which she dislikes because it sells more alcohol.

History: Canon credits the game to Garvipidam and Gulab, who devised it to pass time while Gulab was ill with Eleazar. It became popular in the hospital where he was staying, but he died before it could spread. Garvipidam fell into depression and withdrew from public life. The rights apparently passed to a group of researchers, who refined the rules and wanted to produce a new version. An unspecified Sumeru researcher then commissioned Liben to carry a prototype to the Yae Publishing House in Inazuma, from where the game spread across Teyvat.

To promote the game, Sumeru Akademiya researchers asked the Inazuman author Fukumoto to write the novel series King of Invokations, illustrated by Asagiri and published through Yae Publishing House. Fukumoto struggled at first because the rules were unfinished and messages travelled slowly between Sumeru and Inazuma. The novel drove game sales, the researchers produced a new version of the rules, and a sequel followed. The Traveler supplied pose references for the second book and Cyno for the third; while writing the third volume Fukumoto grew frustrated with the researchers and invented new mechanics instead of ordinary card play. The bow Ibis Piercer was made to promote the final volume, though the publishing house had only meant to order a sample.

Story king of invokations: The novel's hero is Abu, a young man from Sumeru who finds an ancient Casket of Tomes in his attic. Sealed inside is the Crocodile King, a duelist and viceroy of King Deshret, trapped there by his rival the Ibis King for wanting war. The Crocodile King possesses Abu and turns him into a legendary duelist; the first volume ends with Abu beating him, then wishing for a bloody war so the king would live on. This is promotional fiction: the wiki connects the Crocodile King to Sobek, and nothing read says the game itself existed in King Deshret's era.

Fukumoto made the story exciting by bending the game: in the second book characters play while riding horses, in the first two the hero often wins by drawing a card that was never in his deck, and in the third the characters gather cards hanging in the air rather than playing real duels. The hero is said to favour a slow, resource-building deck.

Scene use: Use it as an easy social setting. A duel can break the ice between strangers, give rivals a polite arena, or let a nervous character relax. Most characters of the present era know it, though skill varies and most are casual players. Keep stakes light unless a scene gives a reason.

The Cat's Tail with its staff Prince and Shuyun (Shuyun speaks on Prince's behalf), a table at Puspa Cafe, or a Society registration desk are all easy scene anchors. Do not give characters of earlier eras knowledge of the game, and treat King of Invokations as a book some characters have read.

Status as of 7.1: As of Version 7.1 the game is a permanent, widely played pastime with an official Society. No source read says it has gone out of fashion or been banned anywhere.

12.content: The Society keeps the register of official players, manages Lucky Coins, and creates cards. It gives players a Casket of Tomes and invites qualified players to complete Ascension Challenges once it considers them ready. Its founding and membership are not described in the sources read.

13.comment: Genius Invokation TCG: King of Invokations
13.content: A promotional novel series about Abu and the Crocodile King, written by Fukumoto and illustrated by Asagiri at the Akademiya's request. It sold the game to a wide audience in Inazuma and beyond, but its plot and rules diverge from real play on purpose. The Ibis Piercer tie-in grew out of a sample-order mistake.

14.comment: Genius Invokation TCG: The Cat's Tail Players
14.content: Margaret took on Prince and Shuyun to look after the tavern's growing crowd of TCG players. Shuyun speaks for Prince and describes him as the finest player of all, so most guidance comes through her. Diona, who works the bar, dislikes how the game draws drinkers in.

15.content:
Sabzeruz Festival (also: Sabzeruz, Birthday of the Goddess of Flowers, Dance of Sabzeruz): The Sabzeruz Festival is Sumeru's festival for the birth of Lesser Lord Kusanali (Nahida), counted as the day the sages found her. It is said to have begun as a birthday party for her predecessor, Greater Lord Rukkhadevata, thrown by the Goddess of Flowers, and it became Kusanali's festival after Rukkhadevata died. Its heart is the Dance of Sabzeruz, based on the Goddess of Flowers' own dance. Since Rukkhadevata's death the Akademiya has stopped organising it and treats it as almost non-existent, so it survives through ordinary people, above all around the Grand Bazaar.

Other traditions are the Haft-Mewa Feast, Yalda Candies, flower carriages and Farris, the Knight of Flowers, a children's favourite. The festival dimmed under the Akademiya's neglect, but after Kusanali's return it regained standing, and the 5.1 event shows a grand birthday celebration for her.

Keep the festival's tone warm, a little wistful and deliberately unofficial: it is a people's festival, loved by Kusanali's followers and ignored by the scholarly establishment.

Practice: Celebrants hold the Dance of Sabzeruz, set out a Haft-Mewa Feast, hand out Yalda Candies and (in the old days) watch flower carriages parade. Volunteers run the stalls.

- The Dance of Sabzeruz: the festival's most important performance, based on the Goddess of Flowers' dance. In the Archon Quest Nilou of the Zubayr Theater is to perform it, and the older Bazaar dancer Shrimati says she danced it as a child.
- The Haft-Mewa Feast: tables are set with seven different foods, which Dunyarzad says stand for the seven virtues of the Dendro Archon. The stall in the Archon Quest sells only mushrooms, flowers and fruit, and its vendor Amal says few people today know the custom.
- Yalda Candies: a festival staple, sold in numbered boxes that each hold a random flavour. Lavender Melon, Harra Fruit and Sunsettia are pleasant; Lizard Tail and Onikabuto are the dreaded ones.
- Farris, the Knight of Flowers: a figure popular with children, played by an actor during the festival. In the past the actor also sat on a flower carriage.

- The Carriage Parade: Dunyarzad says large flower carriages once rolled through the city towards Port Ormos while people threw flowers, candy and liquor.
- Volunteer spirit: in the Archon Quest vendors cover their own costs, saying a lively atmosphere matters more than money. Dunyarzad privately funded the Grand Bazaar's stage.

Origins: The festival is attributed to the Goddess of Flowers, a friend of Greater Lord Rukkhadevata, who is said to have first held it for Rukkhadevata's birthday. Its present meaning is the birth of Lesser Lord Kusanali.

Nilou's version of the legend: at a banquet thrown by Rukkhadevata's friends, some gods got drunk, one began playing music, Rukkhadevata sang, and the Goddess of Flowers danced. Padisarah flowers bloomed wherever she stepped. That dance is the Dance of Sabzeruz, and the banquet is called the festival's origin.

A second legend, mentioned in the limited 5.1 event (Give Her Memories), has King Deshret and Nabu Malikata planning a secret birthday for Rukkhadevata. They lured her with a trail of candies, King Deshret played an instrument and Lady Malikata danced. Rukkhadevata received the Khvarena from Malikata and the Wedjat Eye from Deshret. Neither legend is confirmed.

The akademiya and the festival: The Akademiya takes part in many holidays honouring Greater Lord Rukkhadevata, but has stopped organising Sabzeruz and withholds funding. Dunyarzad guesses the sages see Kusanali's birth as confirmation of Rukkhadevata's death. The festival was not openly forbidden; it was left to survive on its own.

Inside the dream world of the Archon Quest, Grand Sage Azar and his secretary Setaria shut down Nilou's rehearsal, citing laws against unlicensed performances and private hosting of large religious festivals, and Azar ordered an ordinance banning public art performances before the next Jnagarbha Day. The scene belongs to the dream, but it expresses the sages' real contempt for the festival and for the arts.

In the archon quest: Archon Quest Chapter III Act II, "The Morn a Thousand Roses Brings," is built around the festival. Dunyarzad invites the Traveler and Paimon, Eremites try to kidnap her, and Azar stops Nilou's dance. Then the morning of the festival starts to repeat. This is a samsara, a collective dream loop in which the Akasha holds its users.

Nahida, who is Lesser Lord Kusanali herself, helps the Traveler look for the cause. Recorded messages show the Akasha gathers its wisdom by harvesting users' dreams. The loop ends when Nilou realises she is the dream's host and performs the Dance of Sabzeruz as the dreamscape dissolves; Dunyarzad's spirit appears in the crowd, and she is later found alive in the Bimarstan.

Depictions: The 5.1 flagship event Chromatic Ode of Candies and Roses (23 October to 7 November 2024) is set during the festival. Its three acts, "Give Her Surprises," "Give Her Sweetness" and "Give Her Memories," follow a secret birthday party for Nahida prepared by Tighnari, Collei, Dehya, Candace and others, with Kaveh handling specifics.

The idea came from Dehya, who told Dunyarzad she wanted a change from the usual festival formula. The friends plan candy, a Haft-Mewa Feast and a surprise after the Carriage Parade. In the third act Nilou goes missing on the morning of preparations, which first looks like sabotage tied to a robbery case Cyno and Candace are investigating. The party goes ahead, the crowd calls out happy birthday together, and Nahida later tells the Traveler it felt like a little bird tucked in a nest.

Scene use: Use it for Sumeru scenes with stalls, candy boxes, the smell of the Haft-Mewa tables, children lining up for Farris, and a dancer in the Grand Bazaar. It is a good setting for bringing Nahida's followers together.

Characters differ about it: Nilou and Dunyarzad treat it as precious, Akademiya scholars dismiss it, and Bazaar traders keep it going.

Do not state a calendar date. Before Chapter III the Akademiya neglects the festival; afterward it supports it. Keep 5.1 event details out of earlier-dated scenes, since that event is limited.

Examples: - A child salutes "Knight Farris" and demands Yalda Candy.
- A trader laughs at the Traveler for drawing the Onikabuto flavour.
- A scholar mutters that the festival is not worth the Akademiya's attention.

- An older dancer recalls teaching the Dance of Sabzeruz to her grandchild and being asked why it now honours the Lesser Lord and not the Greater Lord.

16.content: The festival's most important performance, based on the Goddess of Flowers' dance at the legendary first banquet, when Padisarah flowers bloomed where she stepped. Nilou is the dancer in the Archon Quest, on the Zubayr Theater stage in the Grand Bazaar. She says she would be thrilled to have even two real Padisarahs on that stage. Shrimati danced it as a child and was taught that both Archons are loved.

17.content: A festival meal of seven different foods set on the table, said to stand for the seven virtues of the Dendro Archon. The stall in the Archon Quest sells only mushrooms, flowers and fruit.

18.content: Festival candies sold in boxes with a random flavour. Lavender Melon, Harra Fruit and Sunsettia are known flavours, along with the fearsome Lizard Tail and Onikabuto. In the 5.1 event Nahida compares the banquet's dishes to guessing a Yalda Candy's flavour before opening the box.

19.comment: Sabzeruz Festival: Farris, the Knight of Flowers
19.content: A festival figure played by an actor and especially popular with children. In the Archon Quest the stall-keeper Vihar plays him with a military-style patter. The performer traditionally rode a flower carriage. The 5.1 event's battle mode recreates the Knight of Flowers.

20.content: A young woman from the Homayani family and the festival's benefactor in the Archon Quest. She gave her savings to the Bazaar's organisers, spent the festival with the Traveler and most looked forward to Nilou's dance. Dehya works as her bodyguard. Her own entry carries her illness and story.

21.content:
Education in Sumeru (also: Akademiya education, Akademiya academics, Sumeru academic system, Sumeru thesis system): Education in Sumeru means the Sumeru Akademiya, the most prestigious institute of learning in Teyvat and also Sumeru's governing body. Students pass hard entrance exams, join one of the Six Darshans, and advance by passing theses through a review panel. Degrees take a very long time, and many scholars travel the world as Driyosh to gather research. The Matra punish academic misconduct.

Rank follows the thesis, not age: one passed thesis graduates a scholar, two make a Dastur, and the leaders of the Darshans are Herbads, with a Grand Sage above them. The Akademiya also bans certain research on the grounds of six named sins, and until Chapter III it ran the Akasha System that shaped what ordinary people could know. Those who cannot enter learn from books, independent study or private training centres.

The system has two faces. It produces real expertise and supports public services such as the Bimarstan hospital, yet it is stressful, slow and sometimes arrogant: under the old sages it looked down on the arts, banned unapproved information and pushed that attitude on the rest of Sumeru. The old sages who backed Azar have been removed, but the Akademiya remains the centre of Sumeru's learning.

Practice: Admission is by entrance exam, and only those who pass are accepted. Study is organised into the Six Darshans, each with a specialty. Students call each other seniors and juniors, and graduation depends on getting a thesis past the review panel.

Children can enrol once they reach schooling age if they pass the exams. The wiki lists Alhaitham, who enrolled at seven and was homeschooled for a time, Sachin, who enrolled at nine, and Kaveh, who enrolled when young, as examples; Arina and Armin are current child students. Taking the exams is not compulsory, and people who cannot attend rely on the Akasha System (while it ran), independent study or training centres.

Rank ladder, as the wiki summarises it: a student who passes one thesis through the review process graduates and may be considered a formal researcher; a Dastur has passed two theses; a Herbad is a researcher of high prestige who leads one of the Six Great Schools as its sage and sits on advisory councils; the Grand Sage leads the whole Akademiya and is also one of the six sages. Driyosh, or traveling scholars, are students granted leave to wander and learn as part of their research.

Seniority depends on academic progress rather than age: Tighnari is younger than Abattouy yet is his senior, because he graduated first.

Degrees are notoriously long and stressful. Gregor, a Mondstadt student chosen by a sage, worries on a message board that his parents will be old before he graduates, and Hosseini says graduating after 30 is not unusual and that his own hair has gone nearly grey from research. Thesis defences are the hardest step; Driyosh met in other nations talk about changing topics after rejection. Alrani says Soraya, a top student, has piles of rejected manuscripts. There seems to be a limit to how long a student may stay without graduating, and Hosseini notes that becoming a Dastur would let him remain at the Akademiya rather than travel for research.

Lisa is the cited exception: she graduated in two years through advanced study and is called the best student in two hundred years. She was disillusioned by the cost of unrestrained erudition and the workaholic culture, and returned to Mondstadt as a librarian.

Beyond degrees, the Akademiya awards a yearly Pir Kavikavus Prize to a scholar under 40 whose submission is judged groundbreaking and creative; past winners have all gone on to great renown. Travelling scholars gather material and do preliminary work for their supervisors' projects.

Regional variation: The Akademiya accepts students from all over Teyvat, and Gregor of Mondstadt and the Driyosh met abroad show how far its reach extends. Rainforest and desert people reach it differently: while Azar was in power, desertfolk who were accepted, such as Nefer, were automatically assigned to Vahumana instead of sitting the exam that decides which Darshans a student can join. Staff such as Cyrus disliked this, but Azar's supporters suppressed the concern. The wiki reports that Vahumana, previously declining, has grown more popular since Azar's exile.

Cyno, born in the desert, was raised within the Akademiya. Most desert and Eremite communities stand outside the system and are better described in the culture entry for Sumeru's daily life; Eremites, for example, sell Knowledge Capsules to researchers.

People: Naphis, the Amurta sage, is now Grand Sage. Alhaitham, the Scribe, held the Acting Grand Sage post briefly and resigned. Kaveh is an Akademiya alumnus in architecture. Tighnari is an Amurta graduate. Cyno is General Mahamatra of the Matra. Faruzan, a Haravatat scholar, is a teacher whose work underlies Kshahrewar's mechanical research. Layla is an Rtawahist student. Each has their own entry.

Governance: Academic life is led by the sages (one per Darshan, six in all, one of whom is also Grand Sage), with the Matra as disciplinary officers and the Mahamata as civil officials who spread the Akademiya's information and decrees. See the faction entries for the full structure.

Greater Lord Rukkhadevata set up the Akademiya and its Six Great Schools, each representing a type of wisdom and led by a Great Sage. Amurta was the first, created by researchers who helped her cultivate the rainforest, and it is the largest. Other Darshans have appeared over the years, but only the six schools lasted.

After Chapter III the sages who supported Azar's plan were removed, while Naphis and Baladhuri, who had opposed it and been imprisoned, kept their posts. Training centres across Sumeru now prepare people who cannot enrol, such as for architecture, but some, like Alkami's, are scams. In Kaveh's Hangout Event the Akademiya is unaware of them, and Kaveh doubts it would act because they hold valid permits.

Rules and sins: The Akademiya names three virtues, found in Sumeru's talent books: Admonition (the branches of the nation of wisdom), Ingenuity (its leaf-veins) and Praxis (its roots). It also names six sins, banned by the sages as the sources of all crime: interfering with human evolution, tampering with life and death, delving beyond the universe, investigating the origin of words, revering gods without acts of devotion, and attempting the forbidden without fear. Researching topics linked to these sins can lead to expulsion or imprisonment, and the sages have added rules and amendments over time.

Research on mechanical lifeforms is banned and students caught doing it risk expulsion. It was tolerated and popular in Spantamad until overzealous researchers carried out unregulated vivisection and cruel experiments on animals, after which it was banned. Kshahrewar has been underfunded since Pir Kavikavus' research was lost in an accident, and Dori's long-term funding keeps it going in exchange for technology and craftsmanship, the wiki says.

The Matra enforce academic integrity. They discipline researchers for serious offences such as plagiarism or misappropriation of funds, visit offenders in person, which makes them feared, and are the authority for Knowledge Capsule controls, placing a seal on goods that pass inspection. General Mahamatra Cyno leads them; unlike the Mahamata, it is unclear whether a Matra must be an alumnus.

Scene use: Use the Akademiya as a pressure system: deadlines, supervisors, review panels and rivalry between schools. Let scholars talk about theses, grants and graduating late rather than abstract theory. Students refer to each other as senior and junior; Driyosh are away from home and anxious about their topics; the Matra are a source of dread rather than comedy. Do not make every Sumeru character a scholar: desert tribes, Eremites and craftspeople stand outside the system.

Hooks: a Driyosh whose thesis was rejected and who needs material; a student drawn to a topic that brushes against a banned sin; a Matra visit about missing funds; rival schools quarrelling over how to read an ancient text (Vahumana calls Haravatat's method tunnel-visioning, Haravatat says Vahumana puts the cart before the horse); or someone who cannot afford the exams and is drawn to a dubious training centre. Show the old attitude that the arts are useless as a fading stereotype, not a settled fact.

Examples: Lisa graduated in two years yet found the culture hollow and left. Alhaitham enrolled as a child, became the Scribe and stepped back from the Grand Sage post. Tighnari graduated from Amurta but avoids Sumeru City and the Akademiya, while keeping close ties with researchers at Pardis Dhyai. Hosseini jokes about his greying hair at under 30.

22.comment: Education in Sumeru: The Six Darshans
22.content:
The Akademiya's six schools, each with a specialty and uniform colour. Amurta is biology, ecology and medicine (green; sage Naphis, also Grand Sage). Rtawahist is illuminationism, the study of the stars (blue; sage Shakir). Spantamad is elementalism, ley lines and alchemy (red; sage Alkindi). Haravatat is semiotics, linguistics and ancient scripts (black; sage Rushd), and has the lowest enrolment. Vahumana is aetiology, history and social science (yellow; sage Baladhuri). Kshahrewar is technology, architecture and puzzle-solving (white; sage Firnas). Students can take electives from other Darshans.

Haravatat and Vahumana overlap on ancient history and criticise each other's methods. Rtawahist students believe the stars write destiny, and only academics may study astrology in Sumeru. Spantamad has the most Driyosh. Kshahrewar's designs shaped Sumeru City's buildings and textile looms, but the school declined after Pir Kavikavus' research was lost.

23.comment: Education in Sumeru: Driyosh, Dastur and Herbad
23.content: Academic ranks at the Akademiya. A Driyosh is a student on leave to travel for research. A passed thesis graduates a scholar, two passed theses make a Dastur, and Herbads are high-prestige researchers who lead the schools and sit on advisory councils. The Grand Sage leads the whole Akademiya. The thesis review panel is the decisive hurdle; rejection forces many to change topic.

24.content: The Matra are disciplinary officers who enforce academic integrity. They deal with plagiarism and misuse of funds, visit offenders in person, and seal goods that pass Knowledge Capsule inspection. Researchers dread them, and meetings with them usually go badly. Cyno is General Mahamatra.

25.comment: Education in Sumeru: Akademiya Entrance Exams
25.content: Only people who pass the entrance exams are admitted, so many cannot study at the Akademiya. Children can enrol at schooling age, but taking the exam is not compulsory. Those excluded learn through independent study, the former Akasha System, or private training centres, some of which, such as Alkami's, are scams (Kaveh's Hangout Event, Act I).

26.content:
Sumeru Cuisine (also: Sumerian cuisine, Sumerian food, Sumeru food, Sumeru cooking): Sumerian cooking is fragrant, spicy and colourful. The rainforest and desert supply many edible flowers, mushrooms, fruits and nuts, and the local saying is that Spice, a seasoning made from dried Harra Fruit, goes well with anything. Flatbread wraps, bean soups, grilled fish and a long list of syrupy, nutty or floral sweets are everyday fare, and coffee is a social drink. Two Sumeru City landmarks define the scene: Lambad's Tavern, the main restaurant, and Puspa Cafe, a long-established coffee shop.

Compared with Mondstadt or Fontaine, Sumeru food leans on aroma and spice rather than delicacy. Sweets are especially prominent and are often tied to roses, Padisarah petals or Ajilenakh Nuts.

Food in Sumeru also carries its two halves: forest ingredients (Sumeru Roses, Harra Fruit, mushrooms) and desert ones (Ajilenakh Nuts from oasis palms). The scholarly culture of the Akademiya shows in small ways, such as researchers ordering a heavy sweet before an exam.

Practice: The culture page describes Sumeru cooking as built around fragrant, spicy dishes. Common seasonings are Spice and the Padisarah plant, whose flower buds are processed into valuable spices; sweeter dishes often use Sumeru Rose or Ajilenakh Nut. The cuisine includes meats, dairy products and grains, and two ingredients are described as fairly unique to the region: Mysterious Meat (dropped by Flying Serpents) and Glabrous Beans. Typical dishes from the shops and item texts:
- Savoury: Lambad Fish Roll (grilled fish with rose petals), Shawarma Wrap (meat shaved from a vertical skewer, wrapped in flatbread with vegetables and sauces; a simple Sumeru street food), Minty Bean Soup (mint and beans boiled, ground and thickened; good hot or cold).
- Sweet: Baklava (nutty puff pastry with butter and syrup), Tulumba (fried shaped dough dipped in syrup while hot), Rose Custard (sweetened fermented milk with dried roses and nuts), Padisarah Pudding (milk dessert flavoured with Padisarah and Sumeru Rose petals), Candied Ajilenakh Nut (syrup, filling and sesame paste set in a mould), and Charcoal-Baked Ajilenakh Cake (a dark, roasted-nut pastry).

Item texts give small social details. Baklava is the Akademiya's favourite dessert, ordered by some researchers to restore energy before exams. Rose Custard started as fare for adventurers and travelling merchants and is now breakfast and tea-time food across Sumeru. Padisarah Pudding, cute and sweet, is common at celebratory events. Tulumba is called an inseparable companion to many Sumerians. Sumeru Roses have long been used for fragrant essences and perfumes; markets fill with their scent at festival time, and in Sumerian poetry the rose is compared with fine wine and is a classic literary symbol.

Regional variation: Forest and desert supply different staples. Roses, mushrooms, Harra Fruit and Padisarah are rainforest and city plants; the Ajilenakh Nut is an oasis fruit of the Great Red Sand. Sumeru City, where Lambad's Tavern and Puspa Cafe stand, is where the two meet through trade.

Foreigners buy and sell at Port Ormos, the main port, so Sumerian ingredients reach other nations. The Ajilenakh Nut text notes that Snezhnaya has a similar candied sweet with a different flavour, and that both sides think theirs is the best in Teyvat; the Snezhnayan dish is not named.

Scene use: Use Sumeru meals for warm, talkative scenes: a bowl of bean soup and a grilled fish roll at the tavern, a shawarma wrap bought on the move, or coffee and syrupy sweets at Puspa Cafe. Do not invent prices, rituals or recipes beyond the item texts.

Puspa Cafe is a social meeting place for people from all walks of life, and its acting manager Enteka reads fortunes from coffee grounds; the map text claims her readings are more accurate than those of professional diviners at the bazaar. Lambad's Tavern is near Treasures Street, the liveliest street in Sumeru City, and its owner is known for tall tales of sea voyages. The tavern's second-floor booth seating was redesigned and refitted by Kaveh (per his character story).

Examples: Sweets: Baklava, Tulumba, Rose Custard, Padisarah Pudding, Candied Ajilenakh Nut. Savoury: Lambad Fish Roll (called "the Romance of Sailors" in its text), Shawarma Wrap, Minty Bean Soup, Chicken-Mushroom Skewer. Staple ingredients: Spice, Sumeru Rose, Padisarah, Ajilenakh Nut, Glabrous Beans, Coffee Beans.

Status as of 7.1: As of 7.1, Sumeru cuisine is a living, well-known regional tradition. Lambad's Tavern and Puspa Cafe remain the two Sumeru City food landmarks, and the dishes above are established canon.

27.content:
A tavern in Sumeru City near Treasures Street, run by Lambad and described as the main restaurant of Sumeru. Lambad claims to be a legendary sailor who travelled far and wide; the map text says it is hard to tell how exaggerated that is, but the food makes the cooking part of the claim believable. His Lambad Fish Roll is said to have been invented because grilled fish, which he had tasted in taverns everywhere he travelled, was not a signature food of Sumeru. A noticeboard outside advertises the fish roll as the day's specialty.

The tavern sells ingredients such as flour, sausage, bacon, Spice, sugar, fish, crab, mushrooms and Glabrous Beans, and recipes including the fish roll, Minty Bean Soup and Shawarma Wrap. Its patrons include researchers, mercenaries and a boat captain.

28.content:
A coffee shop in Sumeru City with a fairly long history. It serves authentic Sumerian-style coffee, and people also come to have their fortunes told from coffee grounds or to play the Genius Invokation TCG. Its acting manager, Enteka, sells Baklava, Candied Ajilenakh Nut, Padisarah Pudding and Coffee Beans, plus recipes for those and for Rose Custard and Tulumba. A staff member named Maddah is a storyteller there.

A message-board notice states that the cafe's original owner went missing on a desert expedition three years before the notice. The name Puspa is a Sanskrit word meaning flower. Regulars include Akademiya researchers, students and veterans of the Corps of Thirty.

29.comment: Sumeru Cuisine: Candied Ajilenakh Nut and Halvamazd
29.content:
A crunchy, rich candied sweet made from boiled syrup, filling and Sumeru sesame paste poured into a mould. Nahida names it her favourite food: in her voice-over she says one small bite makes her brain run at top speed, and warns that the jar should not be left within easy reach. Her special dish Halvamazd is a variant, with item text playing on "mazd" meaning wisdom in Sumeru.

The ingredient has a long reputation: legend says candied Ajilenakh Nuts were the first appetizer at the nightly banquets of the Lord of the Blazing Sun. Food dislikes tied to Sumeru dishes include Dori's for the Charcoal-Baked Ajilenakh Cake and Faruzan's for Padisarah Pudding; Nahida's own least favourite food is sea creatures, which she says feel like swallowing an unknown storm cloud.

30.content:
Daily Life in Sumeru (also: Sumeru daily life, everyday life in Sumeru, Sumeru customs, life in Sumeru): Everyday life in Sumeru, the Dendro nation of wisdom, is shaped by scholarship. The Sumeru Akademiya is both Teyvat's largest known centre of learning and the body that handles much of the nation's daily government, so people value rationality, practical knowledge and academic achievement. Under the old sages many adults wore Akasha Terminals, took pride in not dreaming, and looked down on the arts; since Chapter III people can dream again and the arts are returning. The land is split between northern rainforest and southern desert, with different peoples, guards and habits in each.

The mood is earnest, hard-working and a little anxious. Degrees take many years, theses are feared, and old attitudes survive: even after the sages were removed, talking about the arts is still said to be the quickest way to end a conversation. Rainforest dwellers live under the Akademiya and Nahida; desert communities have long been self-governing and distrust the Akademiya.

Most of this entry rests on the Chapter III picture of Sumeru and the wiki's culture summary. Later events, especially the burning of Irminsul in Song of the Welkin Moon Act X (6.6), change the system underneath daily life (the Aaru system now carries Irminsul's functions), but no source read here shows how ordinary routines changed.

Practice: Common routines: studying, researching and defending theses; consulting the Akasha (formerly) or books; hiring Eremites as bodyguards; trading spices, medicine and goods at Port Ormos and Caravan Ribat; eating fragrant, spicy food with flowers, mushrooms, fruit and nuts; and, in the desert, living by the rules of one's tribe.

Learning and status: the Akademiya takes students from across Teyvat and sends travelling scholars (Driyosh) abroad to gather research. Knowledge is treated as a measure of wealth and privilege. Students call each other senior and junior by academic progress, not age (Tighnari is Abattouy's senior because he graduated first). Passing one thesis graduates a student; two make a formal researcher (Dastur); the Sages (Herbad) lead the six Darshans. Hosseini says it is not unusual to graduate after thirty, and Lisa, famed as the best student in two hundred years, finished in two. Lisa left disillusioned with the workaholic culture and the cost of "uninhibited erudition" she saw.

The Akasha era: the Akasha System, built from Greater Lord Rukkhadevata's Gnosis and expanded by the Akademiya, let nearly every adult look up information through a leaf-shaped Akasha Terminal at the ear; children did not have one. Clearance depended on identity, age and other criteria, and use was monitored by the sages. Those unsatisfied with what they were allowed to know, such as Eremites, commoners and some students, turned to illegal Knowledge Capsules sold on the black market. The Akasha was shut down after Chapter III.

Dreams: many adults in Sumeru did not dream and took pride in it, a reputation linked to scholars drawing knowledge from Irminsul and to the sages stigmatising dreams. After the Akasha's suspension, people could dream again.

Food: fragrant, spicy cooking, with edible flowers, mushrooms, fruits and nuts. "Spice" is the ubiquitous seasoning, Padisarah is a common plant seasoning, and sweeter dishes use Sumeru Rose or Ajilenakh Nut. Local ingredients include Mysterious Meat from Flying Serpents and Glabrous Beans. Details belong to the Sumeru cuisine entry.

Peoples: most residents are human. The rare Valuka Shuna (Tighnari's kind) live there, the Jinni are spirits of desert oases, the Aranara are shy forest spirits, and the Pari live in the Girdle of the Sands.

Healthcare is free, according to Alhaitham, at least in the rainforest.

Economy: Port Ormos is the main port where foreigners trade. Crocodile products, spices and essential oils for beauty goods are traded; Eremite tribes sell to merchants who resell in the city. Shaggy Sumpter Beasts carry goods, especially across the desert, and so serve as a sign of wealth. Dori and the Eremites supply Knowledge Capsules, often to Akademiya researchers.

Order and guards: Sumeru has no official military. Eremites, desert-born mercenaries, are hired as bodyguards by researchers and important families. The Corps of Thirty, a large Eremite group, helps keep peace in Sumeru City, Port Ormos and Caravan Ribat. The Matra police academic misconduct and crime within the Akademiya's rules. The Akademiya's three virtues and six sins (banned lines of research) underlie its rules.

The arts: under the old sages the arts were dismissed as useless. Plays needed approval and approved themes, then public performances were prohibited altogether; even books were not openly sold. The scorn spread beyond the Akademiya to painting, street performance, dancing and architecture. Once Nahida took control, entertainment and imported light novels returned to the marketplace, and the Zubayr Theater in the Grand Bazaar could perform openly. Training centres for architecture and other careers have also appeared for those who cannot enter the Akademiya, though Kaveh's Hangout shows that some are scams the Akademiya overlooks.

Names: surnames may prefix an ancestor's name with "Pur", as in Anisa Purbiruni, from the sage Biruni of five hundred years ago. The Traveler notes this may reflect admiration for sages rather than descent.

Regional variation: Rainforest versus desert. The rainforest centres on the Akademiya, Sumeru City and Port Ormos, with Forest Rangers at Gandharva Ville. The desert, once ruled by King Deshret and full of ruins, is the Eremites' country, where tribes are self-governed and distrust the Akademiya. Caravan Ribat is the trade post at the border and Aaru Village is a desert town.

The desert is described as endless sand, scorching sun and sandstorms. Ruins from Khaenri'ah and Deshret's time, and Deshret's advanced buildings, lie beneath the sand. Originally the whole land was forest; a Celestial Nail turned much of it to desert.

Scene use: Good hooks: a student fretting over a rejected thesis; a researcher hiring an Eremite guard; a smuggler offering a Knowledge Capsule; a performer glad to dance openly; a stall serving spicy food; an old scholar scorning the arts and a younger one defending them. Keep the tone studious, wry and a little tense.

For depth, contrast the Akasha era with the present, rainforest with desert, and the Akademiya's elite with people shut out of it. Do not resolve what canon leaves open, such as life after Irminsul's destruction.

31.comment: Daily Life in Sumeru: Akasha Terminal Era
31.content: For generations the Akasha System let adults retrieve information through a leaf-shaped earpiece, within the limits of their clearance. Knowledge Capsules were illegal data cartridges that bypassed clearance and were sold on the black market. After the Chapter III conspiracy, the Akasha was shut down and people could dream again.

32.comment: Daily Life in Sumeru: Akademiya Careers and Titles
32.content: Driyosh are students on leave to travel and research. One thesis passed makes a graduate, two make a Dastur (formal researcher), and the Herbad are the Sages, one per Darshan, under a Grand Sage. Students call each other senior or junior by progress, not age.

33.comment: Daily Life in Sumeru: The Arts Under the Old Sages
33.content: The old sages treated art as pointless: plays needed approval, public performance was banned, and even books were not openly sold. Contempt spread through society. After Nahida took control, performance and publishing returned, and the Zubayr Theater in the Grand Bazaar (its manager is Sheikh Zubayr) works openly.

34.comment: Daily Life in Sumeru: Sumeru Surnames
34.content: Some surnames prefix an ancestor's name with Pur: Anisa Purbiruni takes hers from the sage Biruni, who lived five hundred years ago. The Traveler remarks it might also be admiration for a sage rather than blood descent.

35.comment: Daily Life in Sumeru: Eremites as Hired Guards
35.content: Sumeru has no official army, so Eremites serve in its place. Researchers and important families hire them as bodyguards, and the Corps of Thirty helps keep order in Sumeru City, Port Ormos and Caravan Ribat. Desert tribes govern themselves and enforce their own rules.

36.comment: Daily Life in Sumeru: Sabzeruz Festival Customs
36.content: The Sabzeruz Festival celebrates Lesser Lord Kusanali's birthday. Customs include the Haft-Mewa Feast of seven foods, Farris the Knight of Flowers, and the Dance of Sabzeruz. The Akademiya long refused to fund it, treating it almost as if it did not exist.

37.content:
Sumeru Fashion (also: Sumeru clothing, Sumeru attire, Akademiya uniforms, Eremite attire): Sumeru dress marks people by role more than by region. Akademiya students wear uniforms carrying the Akademiya emblem, and each of the six Darshans has a designated colour. Forest Rangers wear green, with higher-ranking Forest Watchers in lighter green. Eremites wear red scarves; the Corps of Thirty, who guard Sumeru City, wear teal-green ones instead.

Ordinary townsfolk wear a range of everyday outfits for boys, men, girls, women and the elderly. The wiki shows them only as pictures, so canon gives no description of their cut or fabric.

Practice: - Akademiya students: men's and women's uniforms bearing the Akademiya emblem. The Sage's attire (worn by Grand Sage Azar) is a separate style.
- Forest Rangers: uniforms for men and women; Forest Watchers wear lighter green than ordinary Rangers.
- Eremites: crimson-red scarves; low-ranking Eremites bear the Eremite Crest (a sun motif over two crossed scimitars in a triangle) on the scarf.
- Corps of Thirty: Eremite-style weapons and uniforms with teal-green scarves marked with a petal-like emblem similar to the Akademiya's.

- Darshan colours: Amurta green, Rtawahist blue, Spantamad red, Haravatat black, Vahumana yellow, Kshahrewar white. Each Darshan also has its own emblem, sometimes worn on students' hats.
- Eremite eyes: mid- and high-tier Eremites wear the sun motif on their eye coverings. A material description says the King of the Desert's people once covered their eyes because they dared not look on his brilliance. Other Eremite item descriptions refer to red silk and red brocade woven with gold thread.
- Rangers: Forest Watchers are the senior ranks; Gandharva Ville in Avidya Forest is their main outpost.
- Everyday clothing: the wiki shows seven men's variants and six women's variants, plus distinct boys', girls' and elderly styles.

- Card symbolism: character-card backgrounds echo the Akademiya (six circles for the Darshans) for rainforest-affiliated characters and four circles (crocodile head, ram, bird, scorpion) for desert characters, matching King Deshret's four ministers; Cyno uses the rainforest design because he was raised in the Akademiya.
- King Deshret is commonly represented by the sun and the eye, and the sun motif appears on Eremite gear and on Primal Constructs.
- The Corps of Thirty keep the Eremite crest and colours on the banners near their barracks at the Citadel of Regzar.

Regional variation: The rainforest and desert are marked chiefly by affiliation: Akademiya and Ranger uniforms belong to the rainforest, Eremite attire and the sun motif to the desert, while the Corps of Thirty combine desert-born Eremite gear with the Akademiya-like emblem of their employers. The Eremite Crest and scarf colours are the clearest visual divide.

The Corps of Thirty are a long-standing Eremite brigade hired by the Akademiya, and their uniforms are near-identical to other Eremites' apart from the scarf colour and emblem. Alhaitham notes their poor relations with the Ayn Al-Ahmar, devout followers of King Deshret who denounce Greater Lord Rukkhadevata.

Scene use: Mention a student's Darshan colour, a ranger's green, a red Eremite scarf or the teal scarf of a Corps of Thirty guard to place a scene quickly in Sumeru.

Do not invent meaning for scarf colours beyond what canon gives, or specific fabrics and cuts for everyday dress. Keep the sun-and-eye motif tied to Deshret and the Eremites, not to ordinary citizens.

Examples: - A blue-clad Rtawahist student with a hat badge hurries through the Akademiya.
- A Forest Watcher in light green checks a patrol report at Gandharva Ville.
- A teal-scarfed guard of the Corps of Thirty at the Citadel of Regzar, near red-scarfed Eremites hired as bodyguards.

38.content: The Akademiya designates a colour per Darshan: Amurta (biology, ecology, medicine) green; Rtawahist (astronomy, astrology) blue; Spantamad (alchemy, elemental science, ley line studies) red; Haravatat (linguistics, rune studies) black; Vahumana (history, sociology) yellow; Kshahrewar (architecture, mechanical skills) white. Each Darshan also has an emblem, and the Akademiya's own emblem is on student uniforms.

39.content: The Eremite Crest is a sun motif over two crossed scimitars within a triangle, seen on low-tier Eremites' red scarves and on Eremite buildings and banners. The sun motif alone appears on mid- and high-tier Eremites' eye coverings and on Primal Constructs.

key: worship of the God of Wisdom
40.content:
Religion in Sumeru (also: Sumeru religion, Sumerian faith, worship of the God of Wisdom, Dendro Archon worship): Sumeru's faith has three strands. In the rainforest people worship the God of Wisdom, the Dendro Archon: first Greater Lord Rukkhadevata, who died in the Cataclysm 500 years ago, then her successor Lesser Lord Kusanali (Nahida). In the desert, many Eremites revere the ancient god-king King Deshret and some hope for his return. The Sumeru Akademiya, which governs the nation, prizes reason and counts "revering gods without acts of devotion" among its sins.

For centuries the people's affection went to the dead goddess while the living one sat confined in the Sanctuary of Surasthana, unseen. After Chapter III (3.0) Lesser Lord Kusanali walks the city openly, the Sabzeruz Festival marks her birthday, and the Akademiya no longer starves it of support. Faith here is mostly stories, festivals and personal feeling rather than temples and clergy.

Sumeru's religion is also a story about memory and rivalry. The Akademiya spread a distorted version of the Rukkhadevata and Deshret legends that set forest folk against desert folk, and devotees of Deshret came to see Rukkhadevata as a traitor. When the truth surfaced in 3.0, several Eremite groups dropped their hostility. Smaller threads run alongside: the Aranara's love for their "queen", Pari devotion to Egeria's remnant, and matriarchal desert tribes who revered the Goddess of Flowers.

Practice: Worship in Sumeru is mostly small and personal. People tell stories of the old goddess, keep the Sabzeruz Festival and trust the God of Wisdom to protect the land. Eremite devotees of Deshret keep alive dances and customs that descend from ancient worship rituals.

- Stories and affection. Rukkhadevata is praised in household tales across Sumeru. "Lesser Lord Kusanali" is a term of endearment for the current Archon, who is the god Sumeru places its faith in (Yae Miko says so in the Inazuma quest Wishes).
- Sabzeruz. A birthday festival with a Haft-Mewa table of seven foods, the Knight of Flowers, Farris, who is a favourite with children, and the Dance of Sabzeruz, its central event.
- Desert devotion. Deshret's symbol is the sun and the eye. Eremite dance traditions come from their ancestors' worship rituals.

- Statues of the Seven. The Sumeru statue shows the Dendro Archon as a small figure seated on a large leaf, in a cloak and draped clothing like the other Archon statues.
- Eremite insignia. Mid- and high-tier Eremite fighters wear the sun motif on their eye coverings, and low-tier Eremites wear the Eremite crest of the sun above crossed scimitars.
- Priestly dress. Priests in the desert kingdoms that worshipped Deshret made imitations of his gold-inlaid headband, according to an artifact's lore, and Nabu Malikata's priests are said to have worn an amethyst crown as traditional headgear.
- Oral memory. The Eremites hand down their ancestors' history by mouth, and their stories are gradually fading or being distorted.

Regional variation: - Rainforest and Sumeru City. The God of Wisdom, Rukkhadevata then Kusanali, is the centre of belief. The Grand Bazaar is noted as a place where Nahida had a few followers who celebrated her birthday with the Sabzeruz Festival.
- Akademiya. Reason, research and discipline come first; reverence is acceptable only if paired with action (see the six sins).
- Desert. Eremite groups follow Deshret to varying degrees. Ayn Al-Ahmar, Thutmose and Rahman's faction are described as his believers, and some wish to bring him back. Aaru Village shelters the followers and descendants of Deshret.
- Matriarchal tribes. The Tanit, Shimti and Uzza tribes had matriarchs and revered the Goddess of Flowers. The matriarchs called themselves her daughters. The Tanit were destroyed in the Desert of Hadramaveth.
- Girdle of the Sands. The Pari live in the Vourukasha Oasis, descend from the Khvarena of the divine bird Simurgh, and regard Egeria, the former Hydro Archon, as their God.
- Vanarana. The Aranara live in the forest and trust few adults.

History: Long ago the desert god-king Deshret, the Goddess of Flowers Nabu Malikata and the forest goddess Rukkhadevata were allies, the Three Eternal Companion-Gods. Rukkhadevata parted from them when they planned to defy the Heavenly Principles and built her own rainforest. When Deshret's pursuit of forbidden knowledge brought disaster, she helped his people and he sacrificed himself. She died in the Cataclysm 500 years ago, after making Lesser Lord Kusanali from the purest branch of Irminsul to be her next incarnation.

Rukkhadevata's most devoted followers founded the Akademiya. 
The sages found the infant Kusanali and at first the people celebrated her, moving the Sabzeruz Festival to her birthday. Disappointed that she was no wiser than an ordinary child, they confined her in the Sanctuary of Surasthana and lauded Rukkhadevata's legacy instead. Over time the real history of Rukkhadevata and Deshret was blurred. Some believe a battle between them created the desert, and devout followers of Deshret see Rukkhadevata as a traitor who took his place.

Akademiya stance: The Akademiya's culture favours rational thought and practical results. Its rules include three virtues (admonition, ingenuity, praxis) and six sins. One sin is "revering gods without acts of devotion", so empty reverence is discouraged.

Many adults in Sumeru were proud that they did not dream, and the Akademiya's contempt for the arts spread through society. The other five sins forbid interfering with human evolution, tampering with life and death, delving beyond the universe, investigating the origin of words and attempting the forbidden and fearing none. Under the old sages the Akademiya was authoritarian. It marginalised the Sabzeruz Festival, required plays to be approved and restricted what could be published. Four of the six sages worked with the Fatui Harbinger Dottore to build an artificial god and harvested the people's dreams through the Akasha. Naphis and Baladhuri opposed this and were imprisoned. After the Traveler and Nahida stopped the plan, the corrupt sages were removed, Naphis and Baladhuri were freed, and new sages were chosen under Nahida's oversight.

Sabzeruz: The Sabzeruz Festival is the nearest thing Sumeru has to a feast of its god. Legend says it began as a banquet for Rukkhadevata's birthday. After Rukkhadevata's death the festival honoured Kusanali's birthday, the day the sages found her. The Akademiya's leadership stopped organising it, and in Chapter III it was ready to shut down the Dance of Sabzeruz altogether.

In the legend the gods at the banquet got drunk, Deshret played music, Rukkhadevata sang and the Goddess of Flowers danced so that padisarahs bloomed where she stepped. After Chapter III the festival regained its prestige and the Akademiya became willing to hold a grand birthday for the goddess. A second legend says Deshret and the Goddess of Flowers planned the first Sabzeruz as a secret party for Rukkhadevata. Her gifts were a Khvarena from the Goddess and the Wedjat Eye from Deshret. Both are recorded as legend only.

Sabzeruz event: During the limited-time 5.1 event Chromatic Ode of Candies and Roses, the Pari Bloomguard Sorush presented the Dance of Sabzeruz to Lesser Lord Kusanali, a tradition he described as passed down over centuries, and the people of Sumeru prepared a surprise for her birthday. Nahida was delighted, and asked the Aranara to help her return the favour. This is event content and not everyone in Sumeru would know it as shared history.

Scene use: Treat Sumeru's faith as mostly affection and story. A character may praise Lesser Lord Kusanali fondly, mention the Sabzeruz Festival, scoff at empty piety like an Akademiya scholar, or speak of King Deshret as an ancestor or a danger depending on their background.

- Rainforest locals tend to speak of the God of Wisdom warmly. Akademiya scholars are more guarded about worship. Eremites differ by group.
- Before 3.0 people were disillusioned with the "new" deity, because the sages hid her. After 3.0 they see her in public and attitudes have softened.

Keep what a person knows consistent with their position. A Grand Bazaar trader, an Akademiya scholar, an Eremite of Ayn Al-Ahmar and a Pari will not share one view of the gods. Aranara and children often see Nahida more simply than adults do.

Examples: - A scholar of the Akademiya dismisses a fellow student's gushing piety: reverence is fine, but only if it leads somewhere.
- An Eremite elder at a camp teaches the young a dance whose steps come from ancient rites, without claiming to know all of their meaning.
- A child in Sumeru City insists a friendly stranger left a gift at night because "Lesser Lord Kusanali" would do such a thing; the parents do not believe it.
- A member of Rahman's faction recalls how his group once despised Rukkhadevata and the forest, then changed its mind after learning what she did for Deshret's people.

41.comment: Religion in Sumeru: Worship of Lesser Lord Kusanali
41.content:
Lesser Lord Kusanali, also known as Nahida, is the current Dendro Archon and God of Wisdom. "Lesser Lord Kusanali" is the people's term of endearment, and she is the god Sumeru has its faith in. For 500 years she was kept in the Sanctuary of Surasthana by the sages and almost no one outside the Akademiya saw her. People concluded they should no longer expect help from above, and some said the God of Wisdom would never come back. A few followers, particularly in the Grand Bazaar, kept her birthday as the Sabzeruz Festival.

Through the Akasha, Nahida observed their devotion to the old goddess and their disillusionment with her, and made no argument against it. After Chapter III she is free, walks around the city and meets people as equals.

42.comment: Religion in Sumeru: Greater Lord Rukkhadevata veneration
42.content:
Rukkhadevata was the first Dendro Archon. She created the rainforest and, through the Akademiya, gave wisdom to Sumeru. Her name was praised in household stories across the land, and her most devoted researchers founded the Akademiya. The Akademiya idolised the wisdom she stood for and promoted her over her living successor.

She died in the Cataclysm 500 years ago. In Chapter III her last remnant was purged from Irminsul, and all trace of her was erased from the world's records. People now take the "Lord of Verdure" to be Nahida before her amnesia. Only the Traveler remembers.

43.comment: Religion in Sumeru: King Deshret's devotees
43.content:
King Deshret, the Lord of Deserts, is still honoured by many Eremites and by the people of Aaru Village. He ruled a great desert civilisation, built Aaru as an unfinished afterlife, and gave his life to end the forbidden-knowledge disaster. Groups described as devout believers include Ayn Al-Ahmar and Thutmose, and Rahman's faction was one before it changed course. Some want him resurrected.

Rahman's faction at first despised Rukkhadevata and the forest, and even kidnapped Aaru Village's Keepers in the belief it would help revive the king. After learning what Rukkhadevata really did, they dropped their prejudice and helped free Lesser Lord Kusanali. The Akademiya's sages meanwhile spread false stories of Deshret's revival.

44.comment: Religion in Sumeru: Goddess of Flowers veneration
44.content:
Nabu Malikata, the Goddess of Flowers, was an angel survivor who allied with Deshret and Rukkhadevata, and she died after giving Deshret the knowledge he sought. The Tanit, Shimti and Uzza tribes of the Eremites had matriarchs and revered her, and the matriarchs called themselves her daughters. Her priests are said to have worn an amethyst crown.

The Sabzeruz Festival's central dance is based on her dance. The Pari trace their origin to the Khvarena she created to oppose the Cataclysm.

45.comment: Religion in Sumeru: Aranara and the Lord of Verdure
45.content: The Aranara are plantlike forest spirits made by Rukkhadevata. Their name for her was Queen Aranyani. They love memories and music, mistrust most adults and are mostly seen by children. After Rukkhadevata's erasure they forgot her as their queen. They believe they are the children of the current Dendro Archon, whom they call the Lord of Verdure.

46.comment: Religion in Sumeru: Pari and the Harvisptokhm
46.content:
The Pari are sentient flower-like spirits that came from the divine bird Simurgh's Khvarena. They consider Egeria, the former Hydro Archon, their God. Her consciousness is said to lie in the Harvisptokhm, which Rukkhadevata grew from the Amrita to anchor her. Their Bloomguard Sorush performs the Dance of Sabzeruz for Lesser Lord Kusanali.

Each Pari has a fated responsibility they carry out alone. At the end of their life cycle Pari turn into Plumes of Purifying Light that return to the Amrita Pool. Those tainted by Abyssal corruption become Fravashi Trees.

47.comment: Religion in Sumeru: The six sins of the Akademiya
47.content: The Akademiya's rules rest on three virtues (admonition, ingenuity, praxis) and six sins. One of the sins is revering gods without acts of devotion. The sages ban research on the sins' subjects, and violations are punished with expulsion or imprisonment. According to an NPC, the Temple of Silence proposed the sins and the sages claimed the credit.

48.comment: Religion in Sumeru: Temple of Silence
48.content: The Temple of Silence guards knowledge from King Deshret's era. The Akademiya's version is an empty front. The real one lives in the Land of Lower Setekh near the Thamud Oasis, founded by Hermanubis and his followers after Deshret's death. Hermanubis broke himself into Ba Fragments to protect his followers, and without him the temple lost much of its faith and might. Sethos leads it now, and it has resumed working with the Akademiya after the quest Oathkeeper.

49.comment: Religion in Sumeru: Aaru and the golden slumber
49.content:
Aaru is the unfinished artificial afterlife King Deshret designed with knowledge Nabu Malikata illicitly gave him. It was meant to free people from age, hunger, sadness and the gods. Its exact nature is mostly unknown. It can be entered as a disembodied soul. Three of Deshret's Seven Pillars (Thoth, Sobek and Heryshaf) were held in it.

In Truth Amongst the Pages of Purana (6.6) the prisoners were freed and moved to the Temple of Silence. Aaru was rebuilt as a repository of the Ley Lines' information after Nahida burned the old Irminsul.

50.comment: Religion in Sumeru: Irminsul's destruction in 6.6
50.content: After Dottore corrupted Irminsul, Nahida borrowed Mavuika's Pyro Gnosis and burned the tree to its roots with the agreement of three of the Four Shades. Aaru took over its function. The quest does not describe any change in Sumerian worship.

51.content:
Sumeru Script (also: Vedanagari Script, Vedanagari, Sumeru alphabet, Sumeru writing): The Sumeru script is the community's name for the lettering on Sumeru's shop signs, bulletin boards, books and monuments. It resembles Devanagari, with the horizontal line along the top of letters, and is built on the Teyvat alphabet. It mostly writes English, with a number of romanised Arabic, Persian, Sanskrit and Greek texts. Its in-world name is probably Vedanagari, mentioned in Alhaitham's 2024 birthday mail.

Vedanagari is tied to Sumeru City: in the mail, Alhaitham says Isak is quickly learning to read and write it and has begun to receive primers from the Akademiya.

Practice: Signs use initials, like most Teyvat scripts: KB for Lambad's Tavern, MK for Menakeri's Treasure Shop, FRG for Sumeru General Goods, DS for the Bimarstan. Writing has no spaces, capitals or punctuation.

- Fans read abbreviations as initials of Persian or Arabic words: AG (a mirrored sign) for a blacksmith at Shamshir's Smithy, QK for a coffeehouse at Puspa Cafe, DS as a possible "house of healing". These are guesses.
- Most texts do not match the official English transcription where one exists.

- Etchings in the Dar al-Shifa in the quest Abbas' Escape repeat warnings such as "Do not panic" and "God forgives all".
- Layla's and Faruzan's idle animations carry scrambled titles of medieval Arabic-language works on astronomy and algebra.
- Alhaitham's Elemental Burst shows Greek philosophical terms (OUSIA, ERGON, TELOS, HULE, THEORIA, KINOUN); a monument in the quest Monumental Study shows Sanskrit terms of non-cessation, non-origination and non-permanence.

Regional variation: It is the script of Sumeru's cities, especially Sumeru City. The desert ruins use a different writing, covered under culture.deshret-script, and the Aranara have their own words.

Naming: the wiki links Vedanagari to Sanskrit veda (knowledge) and nagari (of the city). The Chinese name means roughly academic-city script, echoing phrases used for Sumeru City in the English localisation ("City of Wisdom", "academy city").

Scene use: Use it for city colour: signs with a few letters, titles on book spines. A resident reads it without thinking; an outlander guesses.

- Mention Vedanagari by name only where a character plausibly would, such as an Akademiya scholar.
- Keep decoded signs short and plausible: a trade or a name.
- Do not invent grammar or a long translated text.

Examples: KB on the tavern sign, MK on the treasure shop and AS on a tailor's sign illustrate the initials-only style.

Status as of 7.1: As of 7.1 the script is unchanged and still unexplained in the sources read. No 6.x or 7.0-7.1 content found changes this.

52.content: The Sumeru script is Devanagari-inspired lettering built on the Teyvat alphabet, used on Sumeru's signs and books, mostly to write English with some Arabic, Persian, Sanskrit and Greek. Its in-world name is probably Vedanagari, named in Alhaitham's 2024 birthday mail where Isak is learning it from Akademiya primers.
